accounts.prose: ExecuteWrapper owns fresh success/failure emitters and exposes their subscription functions. invoke awaits the callback. A value rejected by resultFilter becomes a handled failure `{value}`; any other value becomes `{success}`. A thrown error matching errorFilter becomes `{error}`; a nonmatching error is reported as unhandled and rethrown. clone preserves the two predicates but creates new emitters.

accounts.prose: ExecuteWrapper is a boundary around one attempted call: it normalizes outcomes that a policy is meant to handle into a discriminated object, while allowing an unhandled thrown error to remain an actual rejection. `invoke(fn, ...args)` awaits `fn(...args)`, so the same classification applies to direct return values and fulfilled promises. After fulfillment, `resultFilter(value) === false` produces `{ success: value }`; `true` treats the otherwise successful value as a handled failure and produces `{ value }`. If the attempted work throws or its promise rejects, `errorFilter(error) === true` converts that exception to `{ error }`; `false` emits an unhandled-failure notification when observed and then rethrows the original error. Thus “handled” means represented for policy-level processing, not necessarily that the overall operation ultimately succeeds. With the constructor defaults, no returned value is rejected by result filtering and no thrown error is handled.

referent.description: Clarified ExecuteWrapper invocation, outcome classification, observability, and cloning behavior

qualifications: This describes the captured TypeScript implementation; source text alone does not establish behavior in every built or deployed version.
The ordinary outcome flow assumes the supplied filters and event listeners do not themselves throw; those callbacks are not isolated from `invoke`'s control flow.
`await` assimilates native promises and other PromiseLike results before result filtering.

accounts.prose: The two public event properties are subscription functions, not the outcome itself. A success notification contains only elapsed `duration`. A failure notification contains `duration`, `handled`, and `reason`, where `reason` is `{ value }` for a filtered result or `{ error }` for an exception. For a filtered result, `handled` is always true. For an exception, it is the boolean returned by `errorFilter`, so an event can report `handled: false` immediately before `invoke` rethrows. Timing work is skipped entirely when both emitters have zero listeners at the start of the invocation; consequently, these events are observational and listener presence controls whether duration is measured. Subscriptions return disposables, and EventEmitter invokes current listeners synchronously.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper success/failure event payloads and conditional duration measurement

qualifications: Listener count is sampled once, before the callback is invoked; adding a first listener during that callback does not retroactively enable timing for that invocation.

The duration covers the awaited callback plus subsequent result filtering up to the emission point, and is expressed in milliseconds by either `performance.now()` or a converted high-resolution process clock.

EventEmitter does not catch listener exceptions. In ExecuteWrapper, filtering and emission occur inside its `try`, so a throwing filter or listener can alter the apparent failure path; in particular, this code does not provide observer-exception isolation.

accounts.prose: `clone()` copies configuration but not observation state. It constructs a new ExecuteWrapper with the same `errorFilter` and `resultFilter` function objects. Because each instance initializes its own success and failure emitters, listeners attached to the original are not attached to the clone. This lets a policy variant retain the same classification rules without sharing event subscriptions.

qualifications: The predicates are reused by reference rather than duplicated; any behavior arising from mutable state captured by those functions is therefore still shared.

accounts.prose: Implements the stateful FSM instance and its typed factory. `define` delegates DSL capture, validation and table compilation to `FsmBuilderImpl`, then factories share that immutable-looking definition while each instance owns context, current state, FIFO event queue, timers and tracing state. Dispatch is synchronous at the outer call and re-entrant calls only enqueue; processing runs state begin actions, first matching guarded transition, then fallback handling, with an implicit stay when handlers exist but no guard matches. External transitions run exit, transition and entry actions, committing the target between transition and entry actions; internal transitions run only transition actions. Unknown events and known-but-unhandled events are distinct errors; any thrown guard/action/error clears queued events. Initial entry actions run during construction. The action API loops dispatch back into the queue and delegates keyed scheduling/cancellation to `TimerRegistry`; trace output records events, guards, transitions and actions. The README describes these broad semantics, but its timer-payload promise conflicts with the implementation: the adapter appears to pass no payload argument when `payload` is present and one `undefined` argument when it is absent.

accounts.prose: The practical event algorithm is: enqueue; if another dispatch is active, return; otherwise repeatedly dequeue, reject globally unknown names, run current-state begin actions, try current-state transitions, then run fallback begin actions and try fallback transitions. Guards within one transition short-circuit on the first false result, and transitions themselves are tried in declaration order. A selected external transition performs exit actions and transition actions while the engine's selected state is still the source, then assigns the target and runs entry actions; a selected internal transition performs transition actions without exit, assignment, or entry. Events queued during any of those callbacks wait until this whole event finishes. An event with declared transitions that all fail guards is an implicit successful stay, whereas a known event with no transitions in the current state or fallback produces an unhandled-event error after any applicable begin actions have run.
